items.title: Left pneumothorax — film taken in expiration
items.caption: Upright AP film taken in expiration. The “Sin” marker (sinister = left) sits over the image right, so the patient’s left is on your right. At the top of the left chest is black air with no lung markings, above a thin white line where the edge of the left upper lobe has fallen away from the chest wall — a left apical pneumothorax. The trachea and mediastinum stay central: not tension.
look: The “Sin” marker: patient’s left is on the image right
Left apex: black, markingless air
The lung edge — a thin white line just above the ECG electrode ring
Right lung: markings reach the chest wall
Trachea central; below the left diaphragm, stomach gas with a flat fluid level
teach: Breathing out shrinks the lung but not the trapped pleural air, so a small pneumothorax is easier to see — expiratory films are not routine; an ordinary inspiratory film shows most.
Upright, pleural air rises to the apex; supine, it collects in front and at the base (the deep sulcus sign) instead.
Follow the markings to where they stop — skin folds, the scapula edge and external wires make lines too, but lung markings continue past them.
Tension is a clinical diagnosis — a crashing patient gets decompressed, not a film. Here the mediastinum is central.

quiz.q: Where is the pneumothorax on this film?
quiz.explain: The “Sin” (left) marker is on the image right. On that side the top of the chest is black with no markings above a thin lung-edge line. The black area under the left diaphragm is stomach gas — it has a flat fluid level and sits below the diaphragm.

items.title: Positive FAST — right upper quadrant
items.caption: Right-upper-quadrant (hepatorenal) view, probe marker toward the head. Liver in the near field, right kidney beneath it, and between them a thin black crescent of free fluid in Morison’s pouch. The probe then sweeps toward the liver tip, where more fluid shows.
look: Liver — fine, even texture at the top of the fan
Right kidney — bright central sinus, darker cortex
Morison’s pouch — the interface between liver and kidney
A black (anechoic) crescent there = free fluid
Later frames: more fluid near the liver tip
teach: Supine, Morison’s pouch is the lowest upper-abdominal space, so fluid gathers there first.
In an unstable trauma patient a positive FAST points to the abdomen as the bleeding source — theatre or angiography.
A negative FAST does not rule out injury: small volumes and retroperitoneal bleeding are missed. Repeat it when things change.
Clotted blood can look grey rather than black.

quiz.q: What is the black stripe between liver and kidney?
options: Free intraperitoneal fluid in Morison’s pouch
quiz.explain: Fluid is anechoic (black). Between liver and kidney it sits in the hepatorenal recess — in trauma, blood until proven otherwise. Rib shadows are black bands that run from the probe straight down through everything.

items.finding: IVC traced into the right atrium
items.title: IVC — long axis under the liver
items.caption: Subxiphoid long-axis scan. The inferior vena cava is the dark tube running across the screen deep to the liver, with a hepatic vein above it. The patient’s head is to the screen left: followed that way, the IVC reaches its junction with the right atrium. The probe rocks during the clip, so the view changes.
look: Liver on top as the window
IVC — the dark tube running across the screen, deep to the liver
A hepatic vein in the liver above it
Screen left = toward the head and the right atrium
Diameter change with breathing — judge it over several breaths, not one frame
teach: Prove it is the IVC by following it into the right atrium — the aorta lies deeper and to the left and never enters the heart.
Measure 1–2 cm below the hepatic-vein junction, at right angles to the vessel.
Small and collapsing fits a low right-atrial pressure; wide and fixed fits a high one.
It does not reliably predict who will respond to fluid: positive-pressure ventilation, raised abdominal pressure, RV failure, tricuspid regurgitation and vigorous breathing all change it.
Read it with the lungs, the heart, the patient and the trend — never alone.

quiz.q: A wide IVC that barely changes with breathing most directly tells you…
options: The patient will respond to a fluid bolus
quiz.explain: IVC size reflects right-atrial pressure. That can be high from volume, RV failure, tamponade, tricuspid regurgitation or positive pressure — it is not a verdict on fluid responsiveness.

items.title: Internal jugular vein — long axis and collapse point
items.caption: Long-axis neck scan with a linear probe. The internal jugular vein is the superficial dark tube; the carotid artery runs deeper and parallel to it. Where the vein’s walls come together is its collapse point. With probe pressure the vein flattens while the carotid stays open and pulses.
look: Sternocleidomastoid on top
IJV — the superficial dark tube
Carotid — the deeper, parallel tube that keeps its shape
Collapse point — where the vein’s walls meet
Under pressure: the vein flattens; the artery pulses and stays open
teach: In long axis both vessels are tubes, so shape cannot separate them — use depth, compressibility and pulsatility, and check in short axis too.
Doppler colour shows direction relative to the probe, not artery or vein: red and blue alone prove nothing.
Veins can look pulsatile from transmitted pulsation; an artery still will not collapse.
Where the vein sits over the artery, a needle through both walls of the vein reaches the carotid — keep the tip in view.
The collapse point moves with volume and breathing: head-down tilt or a Valsalva fills the vein and gives a bigger target.

quiz.q: Which finding best identifies the vein?
options: It collapses completely with gentle probe pressure
It shows blue on colour Doppler
quiz.explain: Veins collapse under light pressure; arteries do not. Colour depends on flow direction relative to the probe, veins can pulsate, and depth varies between people.

items.title: Lung point — pneumothorax on ultrasound
items.caption: Real trauma scan over the right upper chest with a linear probe. The lung point is the edge of the pneumothorax: on one side of it the pleura is still (air), and with each breath the lung slides in from the screen right and back out again.
look: The bright pleural line under the chest wall
Where the pleura stays still — only A-lines beneath
Lung sliding in from the screen right with each breath
The lung point — the spot where the two meet, moving with breathing
teach: Absent sliding alone is not a pneumothorax: pleurodesis, apnoea, mainstem intubation and adhesions stop sliding too.
B-lines or a lung pulse where you look rule out a pneumothorax at that spot — the pleurae are touching.
A lung point confirms a pneumothorax, and where it sits hints at its size: the further lateral and posterior, the bigger.
In a crashing patient with absent sliding and no lung point, treat the patient, not the scan.

quiz.q: Which finding confirms a pneumothorax?
quiz.explain: Absent sliding, A-lines and no B-lines all fit a pneumothorax but have other causes. A lung point — sliding lung meeting still pleural air at one spot — is specific.

items.title: Absent lung sliding
items.caption: Linear-probe scan over the front of the chest. The bright pleural line between two rib shadows stays still as the patient breathes — no shimmer. Late in the clip the probe slides along the chest.
look: The pleural line between the rib shadows
No shimmer or to-and-fro movement
A-lines persist below
No B-lines
teach: Absent sliding fits a pneumothorax but is not specific: apnoea, mainstem intubation, pleurodesis and adhesions also stop it.
Look for a lung point to confirm, and for B-lines or a lung pulse to exclude.
In a crashing patient with absent sliding and a tension picture, decompress — do not wait for a lung point.

quiz.q: Absent sliding with A-lines and no B-lines means…
options: A pneumothorax is likely — look for a lung point
quiz.explain: This pattern is suggestive, not proof. The lung point is the specific sign; B-lines or a lung pulse exclude a pneumothorax at that spot.

items.title: IVC collapsing with each breath
items.caption: Subxiphoid scan through the liver. The IVC is the dark band crossing the middle of the screen; it narrows almost to nothing with each breath in and reopens on breathing out.
look: The IVC passing through the liver
Near-complete collapse on inspiration
Re-expansion on expiration
Compare with the wide, fixed IVC of heart failure
teach: Collapse with spontaneous breaths fits a low right-atrial pressure, as in hypovolaemia.
It is not a reliable test of fluid responsiveness on its own, and the pattern reverses on positive-pressure ventilation.
Vigorous breathing can collapse a normal IVC; look at the whole patient.

quiz.q: A small IVC that collapses completely on inspiration most directly suggests…
quiz.explain: A small, collapsing IVC fits a low right-atrial pressure. Tamponade, RV failure and overload all give a wide, fixed IVC.

items.title: Large pleural effusion
items.caption: A resuscitative scan of a large pleural collection, as published. Look for the black, anechoic fluid and the tissue that moves within it with breathing. (No overlays: the published caption does not name the structures, so we have not guessed them.)
look: The diaphragm and liver or spleen below
A black fluid space above the diaphragm
Collapsed lung moving within the fluid
The spine visible through the fluid
teach: Fluid is anechoic; above the diaphragm it is pleural, below it is in the abdomen.
Normally air hides the spine above the diaphragm — seeing it there (the spine sign) means fluid.
In trauma, a haemothorax looks the same; clot can be grey.

quiz.q: Seeing the spine continue above the diaphragm means…
quiz.explain: Aerated lung scatters the beam and hides the spine. Fluid transmits sound, so the spine shows through it.

items.title: Cardiac tamponade — right-heart collapse
items.caption: Apical four-chamber echo in a patient with cardiac tamponade, as published: the free walls of the right atrium and right ventricle collapse intermittently. The clip is one short loop — watch it repeat. (No overlays: the loop is small and we have not guessed chamber positions.)
look: Black pericardial fluid around the heart
Right atrium and ventricle on the screen left
Their free walls buckling inward
The pattern repeating with every beat
teach: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echo: hypotension, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus with an effusion.
Right-atrial collapse in systole and right-ventricular collapse in diastole show the pericardial pressure exceeds right-heart pressure.
A plethoric IVC fits; treatment is drainage — fluids only buy time.

quiz.q: Which echo sign shows the effusion is compressing the heart?
options: Diastolic collapse of the right-heart free walls
quiz.explain: Right-heart chambers have the lowest pressure, so they collapse first when pericardial pressure rises. In tamponade the IVC is wide, not small.

items.title: Pneumothorax — before and after a chest tube
items.caption: Three rows from one patient (the “L” marker is on the image right, so the pneumothorax on the image left is the right lung). A: first episode — arrows on the lung edge — then the lung re-expanded with a pigtail catheter. B: recurrence and re-expansion. C: two weeks after the tubes came out.
look: The arrowed lung edge on the first film
Lung re-expanding with the pigtail in place
The tube tip in the pleural space
The final film with markings to the edge
teach: A small-bore pigtail catheter is enough for most spontaneous pneumothoraces.
Re-expansion is judged by lung markings returning to the chest wall.
Recurrence is common; surgery or pleurodesis is considered after a second episode.

quiz.q: How do you know the lung has re-expanded?
options: Lung markings reach the chest wall again
quiz.explain: The pneumothorax is the markingless space between lung edge and chest wall; when markings reach the wall again, the lung is up.

items.title: Normal lung sliding
items.caption: Linear-probe scan at the right lung apex (the authors’ on-screen note reads “R apex batwing sign”). The bright pleural line runs across the middle of the screen and shimmers back and forth with each breath — normal lung sliding.
look: Two rib shadows — the “bat sign”
The pleural line just below the ribs
Shimmering movement along the pleural line
A-lines below it in aerated lung
teach: Sliding means the two pleural layers are touching at that spot — a pneumothorax is ruled out under the probe.
Check the front of the chest first when supine: that is where pleural air rises.
Sliding can be absent without a pneumothorax (apnoea, mainstem intubation, pleurodesis, adhesions).

quiz.q: What does visible lung sliding under the probe tell you?
quiz.explain: Sliding needs the visceral pleura to move against the parietal pleura, so they must be in contact there. It says nothing about effusions elsewhere or about ventilation being adequate.

items.title: Hyperdense right MCA
items.caption: Admission non-contrast CT: the right middle cerebral artery is brighter than the left — fresh clot seen directly in the vessel.
look: A short bright tubular segment in the Sylvian region
Compare with the same artery on the other side
Brain tissue can still look normal at this point
teach: Clot is denser than flowing blood, so a freshly blocked M1 can show up before the brain changes.
The sign is specific for large-vessel occlusion but not sensitive — CTA is what proves or excludes it.
Calcified or high-haematocrit vessels can mimic it: look for asymmetry.

quiz.q: What does the bright segment represent?
quiz.explain: On a non-contrast scan a single bright arterial segment, brighter than its partner, is clot — the hyperdense vessel sign of large-vessel occlusion.

items.finding: early ischaemic change (loss of grey–white differentiation)
items.title: Early ischaemic change
items.caption: Same admission CT, higher slice: the right basal ganglia and insular cortex have lost their normal grey–white contrast (ASPECTS 4).
look: Lentiform nucleus blends into the internal capsule
Insular ribbon fades on the affected side
Subtle — window narrowly and compare sides
teach: Cytotoxic oedema raises tissue water a little: grey matter loses its slight brightness first.
The deep grey nuclei and insula show it earliest because they have the poorest collaterals.
Extensive early change (low ASPECTS) means a big core already — it changes the balance of risk for reperfusion.

quiz.q: Which structures usually show early ischaemic change first in an M1 occlusion?
quiz.explain: The lenticulostriate territory (basal ganglia) and the insula have the poorest collateral supply, so they lose grey–white differentiation first.

items.title: CTA: right M1 cut-off
items.caption: CT angiogram: contrast fills the left middle cerebral artery but stops abruptly in the proximal right M1 (arrow).
look: Abrupt end of the contrast column
Compare the two Sylvian branches
How far back do the collaterals fill?
teach: CTA locates the clot — the target for thrombectomy.
Collateral filling beyond the block predicts how slowly the core will grow.
Repeat imaging is needed if symptoms change: clots move, fragment or reopen.

quiz.q: What decides whether this patient goes for thrombectomy?
options: A proximal occlusion plus salvageable tissue on imaging
Whether the hyperdense sign is present
quiz.explain: Thrombectomy needs a reachable large-vessel occlusion and evidence that tissue is still salvageable (small core / mismatch), within the evidence-based time windows.

items.title: CT perfusion: core and penumbra
items.caption: Automated perfusion maps 28 hours after onset: a small core (pink, very low flow) inside a much larger region of delayed perfusion (green) — a large mismatch.
look: Pink = core (rCBF < 30 %)
Green = Tmax > 6 s, tissue at risk
The mismatch volume is the tissue thrombectomy can save
teach: Core grows into penumbra at a rate set by the collaterals — slow progressors still have tissue to save at 24 h.
Perfusion maps estimate; they are not histology. Treat the patient, not the colours alone.
Reopening the artery stops the growth of the core.

quiz.q: Why was thrombectomy still offered 28 h after onset?
options: Because a large penumbra remained around a small core
quiz.explain: Late-window selection rests on mismatch: a small core with a large area of delayed perfusion means tissue is still salvageable.

items.caption: Non-contrast CT 24 hours after thrombectomy: a clearly hypodense, sharply marginated infarct in the right basal ganglia and operculum — the final core. No haemorrhage.

Mild local mass effect on the frontal horn

items.finding: malignant brain oedema after MCA infarction
items.title: Malignant oedema
items.caption: After thrombectomy (mTICI 2b), a large left MCA infarct has swollen: sulci effaced, the lateral ventricle compressed and the midline pushed across.
look: Whole-territory hypodensity
Effaced sulci and compressed ventricle
Midline shift — measure at the septum pellucidum
teach: Swelling peaks around days 2–5; younger brains have less room and herniate sooner.
Watch for falling consciousness, new pupil asymmetry or a rising shift.
Decompressive hemicraniectomy, offered early in selected patients, reduces death from malignant MCA infarction.

quiz.q: When does post-infarct swelling usually peak?
quiz.explain: Cytotoxic then vasogenic oedema builds over the first days and peaks around days 2–5.

items.title: Haemorrhagic transformation
items.caption: Serial CT after thrombectomy: patchy bleeding appears within the infarct on day 4 (A), expands and coalesces by day 6 (B), then gradually fades (C–E).
look: New bright patches inside a dark infarct
Petechial first, then confluent
Bright blood fades to grey over 1–2 weeks
teach: Reperfused dead tissue has leaky vessels — bleeding into the infarct is common after large strokes and reperfusion.
Most is petechial and harmless; a confluent haematoma with mass effect is symptomatic and changes management (antithrombotics, BP).
Acute blood is bright on CT and becomes iso- then hypodense as it breaks down.

quiz.q: Why does blood fade on serial CT?
options: Haemoglobin breaks down and the clot is resorbed
quiz.explain: Clot density falls as haemoglobin breaks down — acute blood is bright, then iso-, then hypodense over 1–3 weeks.

items.caption: Six acute haemorrhages: darker swirls inside a bright haematoma (a–c) mark blood that has not yet clotted; d is a uniform haematoma without a swirl; e–f are mimics.

Irregular, heterogeneous margins
Size now vs the next scan

items.caption: CTA of a lobar haematoma: a focus of contrast within the clot (arrow) — contrast leaking from the bleeding vessel.

More than one spot = higher risk

Upper-lobe diversion of vessels

items.title: ARDS
items.caption: Portable film in rhinovirus ARDS: diffuse bilateral airspace opacities throughout both lungs.
look: Bilateral, patchy-to-confluent airspace shadowing
Air bronchograms
Not explained by effusion, collapse or nodules
teach: Berlin definition: bilateral opacities within a week of an insult, not fully explained by cardiac failure, with hypoxaemia graded by PaO₂/FiO₂ on PEEP.

quiz.q: Which ventilator strategy is standard for this film?
options: Low tidal volume with adequate PEEP
quiz.explain: Lung-protective ventilation — about 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau ≤ 30 cmH₂O, PEEP titrated to oxygenation.

items.title: From A-lines to white lung
items.caption: Serial clips from one patient with H7N9 influenza: normal A-lines, then B-lines, then confluent B-lines, then white lung as ARDS develops.
look: A-lines: horizontal, normal
B-lines appear, then merge
White lung: no A-lines left
teach: Lung ultrasound tracks aeration loss bedside, day by day, without radiation.
Scores that add up B-lines and consolidation across zones correlate with oxygenation.

quiz.q: In what order does aeration loss appear?
options: A-lines → B-lines → confluent B-lines → white lung
quiz.explain: Progressive loss of aeration moves from A-lines to separate B-lines, confluent B-lines and finally white lung.

items.title: Hepatised lung
items.caption: Real-time clip of consolidated lung that looks like liver tissue (hepatisation).
look: Solid, tissue-like texture
Irregular deep border (shred sign)
Compare with the liver texture
teach: Consolidated lung transmits sound like a solid organ.
A shred sign at the deep margin is specific for consolidation.

quiz.q: Why does consolidated lung look like liver?
options: Airless lung transmits ultrasound like solid tissue
quiz.explain: When the alveoli fill with fluid or cells the lung becomes acoustically like a solid organ.

pending.title: Confluent B-lines
pending.caption: B-lines merge into a broad white curtain below the pleura (viral pneumonia, child).
look: Individual B-lines no longer separable
Bright band from pleura to screen bottom
Sliding usually preserved
teach: Confluence means more interstitial and alveolar fluid — the step before white lung.
In children with viral illness this pattern is common and patchy.

quiz.q: Confluent B-lines represent…
quiz.explain: As fluid increases, B-lines multiply and merge into a confluent white pattern.

pending.title: Consolidation with air bronchograms
pending.caption: Right anterior middle-lobe consolidation: tissue-like lung with bright moving dots and branches (air bronchograms) — bacterial pneumonia pattern.
look: Lung looks like liver (hepatisation)
Bright branching air bronchograms
Dynamic bronchograms move with breathing
teach: Dynamic air bronchograms mean the airway is open — pneumonia rather than obstructive collapse.
Static bronchograms in a non-moving consolidation suggest atelectasis.

quiz.q: Dynamic air bronchograms favour…
quiz.explain: Air moving in the bronchi within consolidated lung means the airway is patent — typical of pneumonia.

pending.title: VSD on colour Doppler
pending.caption: Colour Doppler echocardiogram: a turbulent, mosaic jet crosses the ventricular septum — flow through a VSD.
look: Colour jet crossing the septum
Mosaic (aliasing) = high velocity
Which side does it start from?
teach: A small restrictive VSD has a high-velocity jet (big LV–RV gradient); a large one shows low-velocity, laminar flow.
Continuous-wave Doppler of the jet estimates RV pressure: RVSP ≈ systolic BP − 4v².

quiz.q: A mosaic, high-velocity VSD jet usually means…
options: A small restrictive defect with a big pressure difference
quiz.explain: High velocity requires a large gradient across the hole — typical of a small, restrictive VSD with normal RV pressure.

pending.title: Secundum ASD
pending.caption: Echocardiogram showing a gap in the middle of the atrial septum — an ostium secundum defect.
look: Discontinuity in the mid atrial septum
Dilated right atrium and ventricle
Subcostal view lines the septum up across the beam
teach: The subcostal view is best because the septum lies across the beam — apical views can drop out the thin septum and mimic a defect.
Right heart dilatation reflects the left-to-right volume load.

quiz.q: Why is the subcostal view preferred for the atrial septum?
options: It is closer to the skin
The septum lies perpendicular to the beam, so dropout is less likely
quiz.explain: In apical views the thin septum lies parallel to the beam and can falsely appear absent; subcostally it is perpendicular.

pending.title: Right mainstem (endobronchial) intubation
pending.caption: Supine AP film in which the endotracheal tube tip sits beyond the carina in the right main bronchus; the airway outline is traced in black.
look: Tube tip below the carina, angled down the right bronchus
Arrow marks the tip; black lines trace trachea and both bronchi
Compare left lung aeration with the right
teach: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical, so a tube advanced too far usually goes right.
Suspect it with unilateral breath sounds, rising peak pressures and falling SpO2; pull back to 3-5 cm above the carina (roughly 21-23 cm at the teeth in adults).

quiz.q: After intubation, breath sounds are only heard on the right and peak pressure is high. The film shows the tube tip past the carina. Best next step?
options: Withdraw the tube until the tip is above the carina, then reassess
quiz.explain: This is right endobronchial intubation; deflate the cuff, withdraw the tube a few centimetres, re-inflate and confirm bilateral ventilation.

pending.title: Endotracheal tube in good position
pending.caption: Supine AP film of an intubated adult with the tube tip in the mid trachea above the carina and clear lung fields; the airway is traced in black.
look: Arrow marks the tube tip above the carina
Carina outlined where the bronchi divide
Both lungs aerated, no collapse
teach: Aim for the tip 3-5 cm above the carina, or level with the medial clavicle ends, in an adult.
Neck flexion pushes the tip down and extension pulls it up, by up to about 2 cm each way.

quiz.q: Where should an adult endotracheal tube tip sit on a chest film?
quiz.explain: 3-5 cm above the carina leaves room for head and neck movement without the tube slipping into a bronchus or up to the cords.

pending.title: Normal chest radiograph (PA)
pending.caption: Upright PA film of a healthy young adult: clear lungs, sharp angles, normal heart size; a reference for comparison with ICU films.
look: Heart width under half the chest width
Sharp costophrenic angles and domed diaphragms
Vessels visible out to the periphery
teach: A PA film is the reference for heart size; portable AP films magnify the heart and can't be read the same way.
Learn a fixed order (airway, breathing, cardiac, diaphragm, everything else) and use it on every film.

quiz.q: Why can't you judge cardiomegaly reliably on a portable AP film?
options: The heart is further from the detector, so it looks bigger
The heart is hidden by the diaphragm
quiz.explain: On an AP film the beam passes front to back and the heart sits away from the detector, so it is magnified.

pending.title: Hyperinflation in near-fatal asthma
pending.caption: Supine portable film from a child with life-threatening asthma: over-expanded, dark lungs with low flat diaphragms and a narrow heart, with a gastric tube in place.
look: Many ribs visible above the diaphragm
Flattened, low hemidiaphragms
Long narrow heart shadow
Hazy patch at the right heart border
teach: Air trapping on the ventilator (auto-PEEP) worsens hyperinflation and can drop blood pressure; give long expiratory times.
A sudden drop in BP or rise in pressure in a ventilated asthmatic: disconnect to let air out, then look for a pneumothorax.

quiz.q: A ventilated asthmatic becomes hypotensive and the film shows severe hyperinflation, no pneumothorax. First action?
options: Briefly disconnect the circuit to let trapped air escape
quiz.explain: Dynamic hyperinflation raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return; letting the trapped gas out, then slowing the rate, restores it.

pending.title: Flash pulmonary edema on a portable film
pending.caption: Portable AP film after a pacing interruption: hazy perihilar and lower-zone airspace shadowing in both lungs, with a biventricular device and leads.
look: Bilateral perihilar haze, worse in the lower zones
Blurred vessel outlines
Cardiac device and leads in place
teach: Cardiogenic edema is typically central and symmetric; treat with nitrates, preload reduction and CPAP or BiPAP.
Flash edema can follow a sudden fall in LV performance, such as losing pacing, ischemia or a hypertensive surge.

quiz.q: Which pattern best fits acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
options: Single lobe consolidation with air bronchograms
Bilateral perihilar haze, worse at the bases
Unilateral white-out with tracheal shift toward it
quiz.explain: Raised left atrial pressure floods the central and dependent lung first, giving a bilateral perihilar pattern.

pending.title: ARDS on VV-ECMO, then recovery
pending.caption: Two supine films from one patient: dense opacities in both lungs when ECMO started (A), and much clearer lungs at ECMO weaning eight days later (B).
look: A: dense airspace shadowing in both lungs
Lines, ECG leads and cannula in place
B: aeration much better, lung edges visible again
teach: VV-ECMO takes over gas exchange so the ventilator can be turned down to rest the lungs.
Radiographic clearing usually lags behind improving compliance and oxygenation.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the ventilator while a patient is on VV-ECMO for ARDS?
options: Normal CO2 using high tidal volumes
Lung rest with low pressures and volumes
Maximum PEEP to recruit all lung
quiz.explain: ECMO supports oxygenation and CO2 removal, so the ventilator is set to minimise injury: low plateau pressure, low tidal volume and low rate.

pending.title: Ruptured AAA with left retroperitoneal haematoma
pending.caption: Axial CTA through a 96 mm infrarenal aneurysm: a bright contrast-filled lumen sits inside a thick grey rim of mural thrombus, with blood tracking into the left flank.
look: Aortic diameter far above 3 cm (calliper marks 96 mm)
Crescent of grey mural thrombus around the bright lumen
Soft-tissue blood spreading into the left retroperitoneum and psoas region
teach: Most AAAs rupture posterolaterally into the left retroperitoneum, which can briefly tamponade the bleed.
A contained retroperitoneal leak buys minutes, not hours: permissive hypotension and direct transfer to a vascular centre.

quiz.q: Where does an infrarenal AAA most often rupture?
options: Into the free peritoneal cavity anteriorly
quiz.explain: Posterolateral rupture into the left retroperitoneum is the commonest pattern; the haematoma may temporarily contain the bleed.

pending.title: AAA rupture site and massive retroperitoneal haematoma
pending.caption: Contrast CT of an aneurysmal aorta with a small contrast blister at its posterior-right wall (labelled rupture site) feeding a large right-sided retroperitoneal haematoma.
look: Bright aneurysm lumen with an outpouching at the posterolateral wall
Large grey haematoma displacing bowel to the right flank
Fat planes around the aorta lost
teach: A focal contrast blister or breach in the aneurysm wall marks the rupture point.
Retroperitoneal blood is a soft-tissue density mass, brighter than fluid on non-contrast images but darker than the contrast-filled lumen.

quiz.q: In a hypotensive patient with known AAA, what CT finding confirms rupture?
quiz.explain: Calcification, thrombus and diameter describe the aneurysm; blood outside the wall in the retroperitoneum proves rupture.

pending.title: Intimal flap confined to the descending aorta
pending.caption: Axial contrast CT of the chest at the pulmonary trunk level: the ascending aorta is smooth and single-lumen while a thin curved flap splits the descending aorta into two channels.
look: Thin dark line crossing the descending aortic lumen
Two contrast-filled channels (true and false lumen)
Ascending aorta has no flap
teach: Stanford B = the ascending aorta is spared; usually managed with heart-rate and BP control (beta-blocker first) unless complicated.
Always check the ascending aorta on every slice before calling a dissection type B.

quiz.q: A flap is seen only in the descending thoracic aorta. Stanford class and first-line management?
options: Type B, IV beta-blocker then vasodilator to target HR <60 and SBP 100-120
quiz.explain: Ascending aorta spared = type B; uncomplicated cases get anti-impulse therapy, with TEVAR reserved for malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain.

pending.title: Non-enhancing left kidney
pending.caption: Contrast CT at renal level: the right kidney enhances brightly while the left kidney (arrow) stays grey because its renal artery has lost continuity (here in a ruptured AAA, not a dissection).
look: Compare cortical brightness of both kidneys
Left kidney uniformly dull, no corticomedullary pattern
Look back along the renal artery for the cut-off or a flap
teach: A kidney that fails to enhance means its arterial inflow is cut off: flap, false-lumen origin, embolus or vessel disruption.
In dissection, branch malperfusion (renal, mesenteric, limb) makes it 'complicated' and changes management toward urgent repair.

quiz.q: One kidney does not enhance on aortic CTA in a dissection. What does that signify?
quiz.explain: Unilateral non-enhancement signals loss of arterial supply; in dissection it defines complicated disease needing intervention.

pending.title: Normal abdominal aorta, coronal CT
pending.caption: Coronal contrast CT of a normal abdomen showing a slim, uniformly opacified abdominal aorta running down in front of the spine with no flap, thrombus or surrounding blood.
look: Aorta narrow and parallel-walled (under 3 cm)
Uniform contrast, no line through the lumen
Clean fat around the aorta, no haematoma
teach: Normal infrarenal aorta is about 2 cm; 3 cm or more is aneurysmal.
A clean coronal view is the baseline to compare with dilated, dissected or ruptured aortas.

quiz.q: Above what diameter is the infrarenal abdominal aorta called aneurysmal?
quiz.explain: 3 cm defines AAA; 5.5 cm (men) is the usual elective repair threshold.

pending.title: Pelvic free fluid on FAST
pending.caption: Suprapubic FAST view from a patient with occult splenic rupture, showing a large irregular anechoic collection of blood in the pelvis above the bladder.
look: Black (anechoic) irregular collection in the pelvis
Fluid outlines bowel and pelvic structures
Calipers measure the depth of the collection
teach: The pelvis is the most dependent space in a supine patient — small bleeds often show here first.
Scan with a full bladder if possible; free fluid is shapeless and has sharp corners, unlike the smooth-walled bladder.

quiz.q: In a hypotensive trauma patient, an irregular black collection behind or above the bladder on the suprapubic FAST view most likely represents…
quiz.explain: Shapeless anechoic fluid outside the bladder in the pelvis is a positive FAST; in an unstable trauma patient assume haemoperitoneum.

pending.title: Internal jugular vein beside the carotid
pending.caption: Transverse linear-probe view of the neck showing the oval internal jugular vein lying superficial to the round, thick-walled common carotid artery.
look: IJV: larger, thin-walled, oval, superficial
CCA: round, thick-walled, deeper
Both vessels anechoic in transverse section
teach: The IJ usually sits anterolateral to the carotid, but overlap is common — always find both before you puncture.
Confirm the vein by compressibility and the artery by its pulsatility and round shape.

quiz.q: On a transverse neck scan, which feature best identifies the internal jugular vein rather than the carotid?
options: Always lies medial to the carotid
quiz.explain: Veins compress easily under light pressure; the carotid stays round and pulsatile.

pending.title: In-plane needle approaching the IJ
pending.caption: Ultrasound-guided internal jugular cannulation with the needle shaft seen in-plane as a bright oblique line advancing toward the vein (arrow).
look: Bright straight hyperechoic line = needle shaft
Arrow marks the needle near the vein
IJ (labelled VJI) as the dark target lumen
teach: In-plane technique shows the whole shaft and tip, reducing the risk of back-wall or carotid puncture.
Never advance unless you can see the tip — the shaft alone can mislead.

quiz.q: The main advantage of an in-plane approach for IJ cannulation is…
options: The full needle shaft and tip are visible as you advance
It removes the need to aspirate
quiz.explain: Keeping the needle in the beam lets you follow the tip all the way into the vessel.
